title: Peace be with you (John 20:19–23)
hookLine: behind locked doors he breathes on them: receive the Holy Spirit
carry: glad, when they saw the Lord

cards: It's the evening of that same Sunday. Mary has told them. They've heard the tomb is empty.

And where are they? In a room with the doors locked, afraid, John says, of the authorities who had Jesus arrested, listening for footsteps on the stairs. Good news, it turns out, doesn't unlock a door by itself.
And then, without a knock, he's standing among them.

teach.b: His first words, in the King James Bible: "Peace be unto you." An everyday greeting, like the Hebrew shalom, the hello anyone might say coming through a door. But look at who's saying it, and to whom.
These are the friends who ran, who hid, one of whom denied him three times. He doesn't start with, where were you? He starts with peace.
Then he shows them his hands and his side, the wounds still there. And John says: "Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord."

teach.h: AS THE FATHER SENT ME, I SEND YOU.
teach.b: Again, peace be unto you, and then a job: "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you."

teach.h: HE BREATHED ON THEM, LIKE GENESIS.
teach.b: Then the strangest gesture: "he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost."
Readers have long heard an echo of Genesis, where God breathes into the first human and he becomes a living soul; the old Greek translation of Genesis uses the same verb John does.
If the echo is meant, this is a new creation, starting in a locked room. Then he speaks about forgiving sins: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven. Churches read that line differently.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians see in it the authority given to the church to forgive sins in confession. Many Protestants hear the power given to every believer to proclaim forgiveness in Jesus's name.
In every reading, forgiveness sits at the center of that first evening.

how: In many churches the minister greets the congregation with 'peace be with you' or 'the Lord be with you', and Catholic and Orthodox Christians link this passage with the sacrament of confession.

o: a Hebrew prayer said at the Sabbath meal
a Hebrew greeting that means peace
a Hebrew blessing said only at weddings

games.q: what's inside John 20:19–23 — tap the pairs.
p: his first words in the room

s: Jesus begins by asking the disciples why they ran away
he begins with peace: "Peace be unto you."
the Greek word for 'breathed on' echoes God breathing life into the first human
the same verb appears in the old Greek translation of Genesis 2:7.
all churches read the line about forgiving sins the same way
Catholic and Orthodox Christians link it with confession; many Protestants with proclaiming forgiveness.

games.q: your friends ran away when you were arrested. now you're back, and they're hiding behind locked doors. what are your first words?
o: I forgive you, but you'll have to earn it.
games.why: his first words are peace, then he shows them his wounds, then he sends them.

practice: Notice your own locked room today, the worry you keep the door bolted on, and as you breathe out, let the word peace go toward it, then toward someone who's let you down, then toward someone you've let down.
If you pray, receive his words as spoken to you, peace be unto you; if not, let your breath carry goodwill.

wordCard.voice: Shalom. The Hebrew greeting behind peace be with you, said by the risen Jesus to friends who had run away.

orig.note: Greek: he breathed on, he breathed into. the same verb as Genesis 2:7 in the Septuagint.

carryVoice: Your line: glad, when they saw the Lord. Peace came first, before any question. See you tomorrow.
